- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository.
- courier:changeset: Trigger when the user asks to add a changeset or document a change: "add a changeset", "document this change", "what changed here". Extracts the consumer-facing meaning of a diff: classifies consumer_impact (behavior-change, new-capability, internal-only) and semver_impact (major, minor, patch, none) per shared/references/delivery/changesets.md's decision table, then writes a summary scaled to that classification. A diff spanning multiple independent topics — common on a backlog/catch-up run, not just a single PR — produces one changeset per topic, not one bundled entry. When the change came via smith, pass along implementer's criteria_evidence — changeset-analyzer uses those exact locations instead of reconstructing approximate ones from the diff.
- courier:commit: Trigger when the user asks to commit code or write a commit message: "commit this", "write a commit message", "commit the staged changes". Reads the staged git diff and produces a conventional commit message explaining why the change was made, not what changed — the diff already shows what changed.
- courier:post-review: Trigger when the user has an already-drafted review or reply and wants it posted: "post this review", "reply to this comment", "mark this thread resolved", "submit my review comments". Takes drafted content — from the built-in `code-review` skill's findings, from `courier/receive-feedback`'s response plan, or typed directly by the user — and posts it to GitHub via `gh pr review` or `gh pr comment`. Does not draft content itself; this skill is purely mechanical execution of something already written, gated by explicit user confirmation before any post fires.
- courier:pr: Trigger when the user asks to open a PR or write a PR description: "open a PR", "create a pull request", "write the PR description". Given a diff, a linked spec, and a linked requirement, produces a PR title and body a reviewer with zero context can act on, then opens the PR via `gh pr create` after user confirmation.
- courier:receive-feedback: Trigger when the user asks to process or triage incoming review feedback: "address the feedback", "respond to review comments", "what do these comments mean", "triage this review". Assembles a review package — diff summary, linked spec, test results, open questions — so the author has full context to respond without re-reading the whole thread. Does not categorize individual comments by priority; that's the caller's judgment call, made with `shared/references/delivery/github.md`'s vocabulary in hand. This is for feedback received on the user's own PR — critiquing someone else's PR is the built-in `code-review` skill's job, not this one.
- courier:release: Trigger when the user asks to cut a release or summarize what's in one: "cut a release", "what's in this release", "generate release notes". Aggregates changeset@2 entries since the last release into a release-artifact@2: filters consumer_impact: internal-only entries, computes the version as max(semver_impact) across the rest applied to the prior version, and carries each changeset's summary through unedited.
- muse:component: Trigger when the user asks to spec a UI component: "spec this component", "draft a component spec", "write a spec for this design", "audit this component spec", "is this component spec ready?", "gate this component spec". Given a requirement@1 or free-text design intent, produces a spec@1 covering props, variants, per-state observable behavior, and accessibility criteria as testable propositions. Every criterion is falsifiable from outside the implementation; error cases and invalid prop combinations carry is_error_case: true. No TBDs anywhere in the document — genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad instead. Gated by a binding exit gate before the spec proceeds to planning.
- navigator:plan: Trigger this skill when the user says "write a plan for X", "how do we implement this spec", "break this down into tasks", "what are the implementation steps", "create an implementation plan", or "plan this out". Also activate when a spec (spec@1) exists and the user is ready to move to implementation but hasn't broken it down yet. Produces a plan@1 artifact where every task includes exact file paths, a brief implementation approach, exact implementation code, the exact tests proving each criterion, a conventional commit message, and covers_criteria linking the task to specific acceptance criteria. spec_file_path and linked_requirement are propagated from the source spec. No TBDs. No "implement as appropriate." Every step is mechanically executable by a developer with zero domain context.
- ranger:audit: Find evidence-backed reachable defects in Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, or Go. Refute candidates, group defect families, and verify fixes against current code and the relevant execution boundary.
- scribe:architect: Trigger when `finding-report@2`, `implementation-review@2`, or `implementation-result@1` identifies a structural defect class. Produce the smallest `spec@1` that makes recurrence impossible or machine-detectable through a type, API, boundary, invariant, lint, test, or CI rule.
- scribe:audit-architecture: Trigger when a draft spec@1 needs checking against the workspace's whole-system architecture — not another spec, and not a single signature — before it reaches scribe/gate-spec: "check this spec against our architecture", "does this fit the system", "audit this against the arch model". Given a spec@1, checks it against the persisted arch-model@2 for boundary violations, competing abstractions, and invariant conflicts, building or refreshing the model first if it's absent or stale for the area the spec touches. Returns specific, rewritten fixes on fail, the same standard as scribe/audit-spec but at system scope instead of spec scope.
- scribe:audit-spec: Trigger when the user asks to review a spec's quality: "review this spec", "is this spec complete?", "audit this spec". Given a spec@1, adversarially reviews it for untestable criteria, ambiguous language, missing error cases, scope overlap with other specs, and incomplete sections. Returns a structured issue list with specific rewritten suggested fixes, not generic guidance. Named audit-spec rather than audit because the bare word audit is already ranger's plugin-level skill name (code/bug auditing) — a different domain entirely.
- scribe:correct-spec: Trigger when implementer reports that a spec criterion contradicts what the system actually does: a spec_contradiction status from smith. Given a spec_file_path, the criterion_id of the affected acceptance criterion, and a contradiction report (what the spec says vs. what the system actually does), revises the affected criterion — and any criteria that depend on it — and returns a corrected spec@1 with revision_note set. Use this when implementation reveals the spec itself is wrong, not merely hard to satisfy.
- scribe:draft-spec: Trigger when the user asks to write or draft a spec: "spec this out", "draft a spec", "write a spec for this requirement". Given a requirement@1 and optionally a research-report@1, produces a spec@1 draft with purpose, scope, non_goals, api_surface (if applicable), and acceptance criteria. Every criterion is a testable proposition; error cases carry is_error_case: true. No TBDs anywhere in the document — genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad instead.
- scribe:gate-spec: Trigger when a spec@1 needs a definitive pass/fail judgment before it enters planning: "gate this spec", "is this spec ready?", "check this spec before we plan it". Default disposition is fail — the spec must earn a pass. Passes only if every acceptance criterion is testable with no vague language, no TBDs remain, error cases are explicitly covered, and scope is narrow enough for one planning cycle. This gate checks the spec on its own terms — whole-system architectural fit is scribe/audit-architecture's job upstream, not re-litigated here. On fail, returns blockers specific enough for scribe/draft-spec to act on without further clarification.
- scribe:spec-drift: Trigger when the user asks whether implemented code still matches its spec, weeks or months after implementation: "check spec drift", "does the code still match this spec?", "has this spec drifted?". Given a spec@1 (via spec_file_path) and a workspace root, reads the spec from disk and the implementation from the workspace, and reports each criterion as covered (implemented and tested), uncovered (no matching implementation), or drifted (implementation exists but diverges from the criterion's contract). This is an on-demand diagnostic, not a blocking gate — scribe/gate-spec is the blocking gate.
- scribe:verify-spec: Trigger when the user asks whether a spec matches its source: "is this grounded?", "does this spec match the requirement?", "check this spec against the requirement". Given a draft spec@1 plus the originating requirement@1 and optional research-report@1, checks whether each acceptance criterion is grounded in the source artifacts. Classifies criteria as supported, unsupported, or overfitted. Collects evidence only — does not produce a pass/fail verdict. Use before implementation, not after — for post-implementation drift, use scribe/spec-drift instead.
- sentinel:gate: Trigger this skill when the user says "verify this", "check this spec", "check this plan", "check this requirement", "check this PR", "is this done?", "review this for completeness", "does this meet the criteria?", "gate this", or "quality check" — also before stage transitions: starting implementation from a spec, shipping from an implementation, opening a PR from a branch. Applies to any stage artifact: requirements, specs, plans, implementations, PRs. Do not activate for general Q&A, code explanation, or exploratory work with no artifact boundary being crossed. The gate either clears the artifact for the next stage or returns specific, actionable blockers to the producing agent.
- smith:implement: Activate for implementation, implementation tests, or behavior-preserving refactoring. Execute bounded batches with risk-based verification, defect-family review, and an independent scoped verdict. Do not activate for explanation-only requests.
- vanguard:research: Activate when the user says "I need to understand X before deciding", "is there a way to do Y", "what are the options for Z", "research this", "investigate this", "what does the codebase already do for X", "prior art on Y", or "what are the risks of approach Z" — also when the approach for a spec or plan is unclear, when checking what dependencies exist for a feature, or when any design question needs an evidence base before commitment. Investigates the question across internal sources (specs, docs, codebase patterns, manifests) and external sources as needed, then produces a research-report@1 that distinguishes confirmed findings from likely inferences from unverified assumptions, with a falsifiable recommendation and explicit confidence level so a spec writer (scribe) isn't surprised by implementation reality.
- weaver:audit-backlog: Trigger when the user asks about overall backlog health: "what's in the backlog", "audit the backlog", "what requirements are missing coverage". Cross-references all open requirement@1 objects against existing specs and implementation files. Returns per-requirement status (covered, partial, missing, duplicate) with evidence, plus a structured summary — per-status counts and an optional one-clause note, not a prose paragraph. Named audit-backlog rather than bare audit because that word is already ranger's plugin-level skill name (code/bug auditing) — a different domain entirely.
- weaver:capture-need: Trigger when the user describes a raw need in free text: "we need X", "the problem is Y", "users are asking for Z". Converts unstructured text into a structured requirement@1 draft — id, statement, stakeholder, why, done_when — without asking clarifying questions. Fields that cannot be inferred are omitted, not fabricated. out_of_scope is intentionally left empty for weaver/connect-requirement or a human to fill in.
- weaver:clarify-requirement: Trigger when a requirement@1 draft from weaver/capture-need has gaps to close before a spec can be written: "is this requirement complete?", "what's missing from this requirement". Given a requirement@1, evaluates gaps in priority order — testability of done_when, specificity of stakeholder, explicitness of out_of_scope — and either asks one focused question or returns the completed requirement with out_of_scope populated. One question per invocation, never a list.
- weaver:connect-requirement: Trigger when the user asks whether a specific requirement already exists or relates to other work: "is this already captured?", "does this overlap with an existing requirement?", "what does this relate to?". Given one requirement@1 (or a small named set), searches the workspace for related specs and implementation files, and checks for duplicate or overlapping requirements. Returns coverage status and duplicate_of references scoped to just the requirement(s) given — not a full backlog sweep.
- weaver:prioritize-backlog: Trigger when the user asks what to work on first from a set of requirements: "what should we prioritize", "rank the backlog", "what's most urgent". Given a list of requirement@1 drafts, ranks them by impact, urgency, and dependency order — a requirement another depends on ranks above the one depending on it, even if its own impact/urgency score is lower. Returns an ordered list with a concrete rationale per requirement.
- mason:audit-plugin: Audit an existing plugin against repository authoring, schema, wiring, and packaging rules. Use for plugin conformance or release-readiness checks. Return an evidence-backed pass, fail, or warning for each check without modifying files.
- mason:design-schema: Trigger when the user wants to design a new inter-agent artifact schema: "design a schema for X", "add a new schema to shared/schemas", "what should this handoff look like?". Given a description of what the artifact represents, who produces it, and who consumes it, produces a JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) following ecosystem conventions — $id as name@version, additionalProperties false, a reasoning scratchpad field, all fields documented — and checks for conflicts with existing schemas.
- mason:evaluate: Evaluate a plugin workflow against a fixed behavioral fixture. Use for release gates, Claude/Codex comparisons, regression checks, and longitudinal plugin quality analysis. Preserve exact execution provenance and hidden-oracle isolation.
- mason:scaffold-plugin: Create a complete plugin from an ID and purpose. Use for new plugin requests. Generate the manifest, skill, cognitive-mode agents, shared linkage, routing, and any required schema contracts; validate the result before handoff.
- mason:scaffold-subagent: Add one conformant agent to an existing plugin. Use when the request names an agent task and tier without requesting a new plugin. Create only the agent file and report required routing; leave unrelated plugin files unchanged.
- cowork-plugin-management:cowork-plugin-customizer: Customize a Claude Code plugin for a specific organization's tools and workflows. Use when: customize plugin, set up plugin, configure plugin, tailor plugin, adjust plugin settings, customize plugin connectors, customize plugin skill, tweak plugin, modify plugin configuration.
- cowork-plugin-management:create-cowork-plugin: Guide users through creating a new plugin from scratch in a cowork session. Use when users want to create a plugin, build a plugin, make a new plugin, develop a plugin, scaffold a plugin, start a plugin from scratch, or design a plugin. This skill requires Cowork mode with access to the outputs directory for delivering the final .plugin file.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a live pane, band, status line, toast or hook inside Claude Code (terminal or desktop Code tab), written as a plugin of function hooks that hot-reloads in this session. Load before writing or debugging a hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- anthropic-skills:built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:computer-use: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills.
- anthropic-skills:deep-research: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly.
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf
- anthropic-skills:pptx
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator
- anthropic-skills:xlsx

# Agent guide

Rules for AI agents working in this repo.

## Crates

| Crate | License | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| callisto-model | MIT | none |
| callisto-manifests | FSL-1.1-MIT | model |
| callisto-graph | FSL-1.1-MIT | model, manifests |
| callisto-cli | FSL-1.1-MIT | model, manifests, graph |
| callisto-fixtures | FSL-1.1-MIT | model (dev-only) |

- `callisto-model` (MIT) must never depend on an FSL crate.
- Check with `grep -H "^license" crates/*/Cargo.toml` after adding or moving a crate.

## Commands

- Full pipeline: `just ci` (includes the 90% coverage gate). `just test`, `just lint`, `just fmt`.
- Scoped iteration: one `cargo test -p <crate>` or `cargo clippy -p <crate> --all-targets -- -D warnings` at a time.
  - Not `moon run <project>:test`: its per-project fan-out serializes on `target/`'s build lock.
  - Never run cargo builds in parallel.
- Changesets: `callisto add --package callisto-cli:<bump> --summary "..."` (non-interactive). Target `callisto-cli`: its changelog is the one users read. One changeset per user-visible topic, written as the changelog entry: what the user sees now, no internal names or mechanism.
- Never `git checkout -- Cargo.lock` as cleanup. A lockfile diff means investigate, not discard.

## Invariants

1. Safe Rust only: `unsafe_code = "forbid"`.
2. Manifest edits preserve format: `toml_edit` for TOML; JSON keeps key order and fingerprinted indentation. No regex or line edits.
3. File writes go through `callisto_model::atomic::atomic_write`.
4. User-facing errors derive `miette::Diagnostic` with a code and a fix.
5. No emojis in docs or code.
6. No cargo features in shipped crates; behaviour is chosen at runtime (#143). The dev-only `callisto-model/test-util` feature is the exception.

## Fixing bugs

- Grep for structurally identical code (same algorithm, other file, ecosystem or mode). A sibling with the same defect is in scope now.
- N copies of one logic: unify to one implementation rather than patching each.
- A deliberately deferred sibling gets an explicit record: changeset note, tracked follow-up or code comment.
- A new shared helper migrates every call site in the same change, or the rest are tracked.

## Specs and plans

- Specs (`spec@1`) live in `docs/specs/`, one per area, current behavior only. Change the spec in the same PR as the behavior. No history, rationale or revision notes.
- This repo's release workflow has no GitHub Environment or reviewer gate and only `execute` gets registry secrets (owner policy, enforced by `.github/tests/verify-release-workflow-policy.sh`). Never add one.
- Read `ARCHITECTURE.md` and the matching `docs/architecture/` topic before changing behavior in an area.
- Read `docs/adr/README.md` before changing release flow, Git access, publishing, distribution, platform packages or manifest writes. Reversing an ADR needs a new ADR the owner accepts.
- Plans (`plan@1`) live in `docs/projects/`. Delete a plan once its work ships.

import subprocess

G = '/usr/bin/git'
base = '/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/'

    return subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=cwd)

fix(release): derive one tag, forge release and forge publish per package

A package with several release identities, such as a Cargo and npm package in one directory, derived a tag, forge release and forge publish operation for every identity although they address one physical tag and one GitHub release. With release assets configured the same artifact slot was derived once per identity, so `release` failed to plan with a repeated artifact slot.

Each package now has an owner, its first selected identity in manifest order, and only the owner carries the tag, forge release, forge publish and uploads. The tag still waits for the registry publishes of every selected identity. Selecting one identity of a dual package makes it the owner. Intent and receipt schema versions are unchanged: an intent derived before this change differs from a fresh derivation and fails closed as stale.

A package with several release identities, such as a Cargo and npm package in one directory, derived a tag, forge release and forge publish for every identity, though they address one physical tag and one GitHub release. With `[[release.artifact]]` configured, the same artifact slot was also derived once per identity, so a dual product could not plan a release.

Reproduced on `main` with the real binary: a dual Cargo/npm product with one release asset fails `callisto release --dry-run` with `release intent repeats an artifact slot` (E158). With this change the same workspace plans one tag, one draft release, one upload and one publish, under `cargo/dual`, and `npm/dual` publishes to npm.

What changes:
- Each package has an owner: its first selected identity in manifest order (Cargo, then npm, then PyPI). Only the owner carries the tag, forge release, forge publish and uploads.
- The tag still waits for the registry publishes of every selected identity, so a dual package's tag and release follow both publishes.
- Selecting one identity (`--package npm/dual`) makes it the owner. The plan for each single-identity selection is unchanged from `main`.
- Registry publishes stay one per identity.

No wire change. Intent, envelope and receipt keep their versions. An intent derived before this change differs from a fresh derivation and fails closed as stale, before any provider is touched, and `release plan` rebuilds it. Single-identity intents are byte-identical.

Tests: the dual-owner snapshot loses exactly the npm tag, forge release and forge publish operations. New tests check one operation of each kind on the owner, a partial selection owned by the selected identity, and a dual product with an artifact deriving one upload that the forge publish waits for. `just ci` passes.

content.content:
---

## Python (PyPI)

Publishing uses `twine upload`, which reads `TWINE_USERNAME` (`__token__` for a PyPI API token) and `TWINE_PASSWORD` (the token value):

```yaml
env:
  TWINE_USERNAME: __token__
  TWINE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PYPI_TOKEN }}
```

Do not use `TWINE_API_TOKEN` — twine does not recognize that variable name.

Map the generated workflow's `PYPI_TOKEN` secret to `TWINE_PASSWORD` in the publishing job. The secret name alone does not configure Twine.

### Generated Callisto workflows

Generated release workflows accept `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN`, `NPM_TOKEN`, and `PYPI_TOKEN` as secrets. They supply each token only during publishing. Custom npm registries need their own native configuration.

Native publish hooks, including `prepare` and `prepublishOnly`, run unchanged with their usual publishing environment.

### Current Python support limits

Callisto supports static PEP 621 or Poetry versions with `python -m build` and Twine. Current limits:

- Co-located Cargo/Maturin projects fail discovery with E007, including Cargo-owned dynamic Python versions.
- Registry observation checks version presence, not the complete wheel/sdist set. A retry can skip files after a partial upload.
- One configured URL serves both simple-index reads and Twine uploads. Private indexes with separate routes, read authentication, or HTML-only responses need explicit support. Twine credentials do not authenticate `curl`.
- Snapshots use a PEP 440 local label (`0.0.0.dev0+<tag>.<sha>`), which public PyPI rejects. See [PEP 440](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/version-specifiers/).

content.text:
Cleanup and the collapse are done, and the Python summary is below.

## Cleanup
I removed 13 stale worktrees (clean, pushed, PR merged), losing nothing. A batch removal that included forced deletions and unpushed branches was denied as irreversible, so I left those alone. These remain for you to decide:
- **Unpushed local commits:** `stack-ci`, `wave1-stack` and `wave2-base`. Their PRs merged, but the local tips aren't on any remote branch.
- **Detached or base worktrees:** `w2-sys-retry` and `wave1-base`, both at or behind `main`.
- **Stale untracked file:** `wf_cd627354-1a0-2`, which holds an old draft of a test #227 already merged.
- **Locked:** `fix-gh-credentials`.
- **My previous worktrees:** `owner-history` is now unused, and I'm working in `one-op-per-owner`.

## Shared effects: PR #231
A package with several identities now has one owner that carries its single tag, GitHub release, publish and uploads.
- **Real-binary check:** the dual Cargo/npm product that failed to plan with "repeated artifact slot" now plans, with each of those operations appearing once under `cargo/dual`.
- **Partial selections:** they plan exactly as before.
- **Wire and tests:** there is no wire change, and `just ci` passes. It has not had an independent review. It is small, but you've seen what the last review found.

## Python today
| Area | State |
| --- | --- |
| Discovery and versions | Static PEP 621 and Poetry versions work, with normalized names. Dynamic versions fail with E007. |
| Dependency tracking | Works for `[project].dependencies`, every extra, and Poetry's main table. Each declaration is rewritten by its own constraint, with markers kept. |
| Release | Builds with `python -m build`, uploads with twine, and observes via the simple index. |
| Gaps | A partial upload is adopted as complete. Reads and uploads share one URL. Snapshot versions are rejected by PyPI. Maturin is unsupported. Hosted publication has never run. |

## File sets (W3)
The design I'd build is about 400-600 lines in one PR, with no wire change:
- Build once into a cleaned directory and inventory the files with their hashes.
- Classify against the index's per-file hashes and yanked state.
- Upload only the missing files, by explicit list.
- Retry confirmation for minutes, because PyPI caches the index for 10 minutes.
- Treat a yanked file in the set as a Conflict.
- Fix two existing hazards: a stale `dist/` is uploaded, and the glob for `1.0` also matches `1.0.1*`.

I still need your answers on three decisions:
- **Build inside `execute`, with manifest binding later:** my recommendation is yes.
- **A rerun counts a present file by name only:** my recommendation is yes.
- **Extra remote files are ignored:** my recommendation is yes.

## Dependency groups
Defer. They aren't tracked today, but uv ignores or rejects version pins for workspace members, and Poetry siblings are path dependencies with no version to go stale. If you want it, it is about 100 lines, treated as `Dev`.

needs input: answers on the three W3 decisions, whether to defer dependency groups, and what to do with the six remaining worktrees.

input.description: Prior art: multi-artifact release pipelines
input.name: research-pipelines
input.prompt:
Web research task, read-only (do not edit repo files). Use WebSearch (mode "extended" for hard facts) and WebFetch to read PRIMARY sources: official docs, design docs, and source code on GitHub (raw.githubusercontent.com or docs sites), not blog summaries. Cite a URL for every claim; say which claims you could not confirm from a primary source. Today is 2026-10-16; prefer current behavior and give versions.

Context: Callisto is a Rust release manager for polyglot monorepos (Cargo, npm, PyPI). Its model: plan (derive an immutable intent from a committed decision) -> build (CI matrix, no secrets) -> execute (only job with registry secrets). Operations are a DAG: registry publishes per ecosystem, then ONE git tag, then a draft GitHub release, asset uploads, then publish of the release (the public announcement happens only after every required publish and upload). Recovery has no journal: a rerun re-derives the same operations and observes the remote (registry, git, forge) to see what already happened, then does only what is missing. Open design questions: (1) should the set of files for a Python release be bound by a sealed manifest (names + sha256) produced by a build job, or just built in the publish job; (2) how a rerun should treat files that already exist remotely; (3) how to make shared effects (tag, GitHub release) happen once for a package that publishes to several registries.

Write the full report to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-callisto/15c732d1-457b-4efc-91e5-664943f21b1c/scratchpad/research-pipelines.md (under 2500 words) and make your final message a summary under 700 characters naming the file. Do not paste the report into the final message.

Investigate how these tools handle building artifacts once, binding them, publishing to several destinations, announcing only after everything succeeded, and recovering from a partial failure:
1. cargo-dist (axodotdev/cargo-dist, now `dist`): plan/build/host/publish/announce phases, dist-manifest.json (what it records, who consumes it), how artifacts move between CI jobs, what happens on partial failure and re-run, whether the announce/GitHub release step waits for all publish jobs, how checksums are handled, how it detects already-published work.
2. GoReleaser (and GoReleaser Pro split/merge): `--split`/`--merge`, `dist/` metadata files, release `draft`/`replace_existing_artifacts`/`use_existing_draft`/`keep_existing_drafts`, behavior when the release or an asset already exists, `--skip=publish`, partial publish recovery, checksum file, whether publishing to blob/brew/etc. is ordered and what happens if one publisher fails.
3. release-please (manifest mode, GitHub Action): how releases/tags get created, and the known "tag created but publish failed" recovery story; and Changesets (`changeset publish`, `changesets/action`): how it publishes, tags only successful publishes, treats already-published as success, retry model.
4. semantic-release: `@semantic-release/github` asset upload, behavior when upload fails mid-way, and `--dry-run`; python-semantic-release `publish` command and its PyPI/GitHub asset flow, and how it recovers.
5. PyPI's recommended pattern and cibuildwheel's recommended workflow: build_wheels matrix + build_sdist -> a single upload job `needs` both -> downloads all artifacts -> publishes once; pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish usage (trusted publishing, `skip-existing`, attestations). Read the packaging.python.org "publishing with GitHub Actions" guide and cibuildwheel's docs.

For each tool give a 3-6 line summary of the mechanism, then end with: (a) patterns worth copying for Callisto's three open questions, (b) mistakes or limitations of these tools Callisto can avoid, (c) where Callisto's observe-the-remote, no-journal recovery is stronger or weaker than each tool's approach. Be specific and quote short key phrases from docs where they matter.

input.description: Modern PyPI publishing and provenance
input.name: research-pypi
input.prompt:
Web research task, read-only (do not edit repo files). Use WebSearch (mode "extended" for hard facts) and WebFetch to read PRIMARY sources: PyPI/Warehouse docs and source, PEPs, packaging.python.org, tool source on GitHub (raw.githubusercontent.com), not blog summaries. Cite a URL for every claim; say which you could not confirm from a primary source. Today is 2026-10-16; prefer current behavior and give versions.

Context: Callisto is a Rust release manager for polyglot monorepos. For Python it currently builds with `python -m build --sdist --wheel` inside the job that holds the registry token, uploads with `twine upload dist/<name>-<version>*` (with --skip-existing only on default PyPI/TestPyPI), and observes completion by reading the PyPI simple index JSON and treating ANY one matching non-yanked file as the whole release being published, so a partial upload is adopted as complete. It has no support for trusted publishing (OIDC) or attestations, and snapshot versions use PEP 440 local labels that PyPI rejects. It records no file digests. The release also gets a git tag and GitHub release only after the registry publish is confirmed.

Write the full report to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-callisto/15c732d1-457b-4efc-91e5-664943f21b1c/scratchpad/research-pypi.md (under 2500 words) and make your final message a summary under 700 characters naming the file. Do not paste the report into the final message.

Answer, with primary-source evidence:
1. Trusted publishing (OIDC) today: how it works, which CI providers, why PyPI recommends it over API tokens, whether it works from a self-hosted CLI tool (not only the pypa action), and what a non-Python tool must do to use it (token exchange endpoint, `twine`/`uv publish --trusted-publishing`). Does uv publish support it natively, and what does that imply for a Rust tool that shells out to twine or uv?
2. Attestations (PEP 740): how generated, what is signed, how they are uploaded and displayed, how consumers verify them, which tools produce them (pypi-attestations, gh-action-pypi-publish, uv publish), and whether attestations exist per file. Could a release tool bind its own file manifest to attestations?
3. `uv publish` internals: how it decides a file already exists (`--check-url`), hash comparison, retry semantics and what exit codes mean; whether it is idempotent for identical files; read the source (crates/uv-publish) to confirm. Is `uv build` + `uv publish` a better default pair than `python -m build` + twine? What does `uv build` do about reproducibility (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH)?
4. The PyPI 14-day new-file restriction: confirm from a PyPI blog or docs page (primary), exact scope (new files on older releases), the error text if documented, and whether a "release in progress" state exists in the API.
5. PyPI index freshness: JSON API vs simple API cache headers and CDN purge on upload (Warehouse source: surrogate-key purge); how long after upload a file is visible in each; what tools use to wait (e.g. pip, uv, poetry retry on 404).
6. Yank semantics (PEP 592) per file, and what the JSON API reports for a release whose files are partly yanked.
7. Deterministic builds: which common backends are reproducible by default (hatchling, poetry-core, flit-core, setuptools, pdm-backend, maturin) and what SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH does for each. I already measured with `uv build` that hatchling and poetry-core are byte-identical across timestamp changes, pdm-backend wheel identical but sdist not, setuptools neither; confirm against backend docs and say whether setting SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH to the commit time would make a release tool's rebuilds comparable.
8. What would a best-in-class release tool do for a Python release to prove completeness and integrity? Give a concrete protocol (declared set, digests, per-file observation, attestation, retry) and note which steps no existing tool does.

End with a short list of the claims you could not verify.

content.content:
1	# Prior art: multi-artifact release pipelines (2026-10-16)
2	
3	Bracketed keys like [D1] map to the URL list at the end. All were read from primary sources (docs or source on GitHub main at read time). "Unconfirmed" marks what I could not verify from a primary source. "Inference" marks my reading of code, not tested behavior.
4	
5	Versions read: dist 0.33.0 (2026-09-10); GoReleaser main (v2.19 nightlies; split/merge is Pro and its code is not in the OSS repo); release-please 17.11.2, release-please-action 5.0.0; @changesets/cli 3.0.3, changesets/action 2.1.2; python-semantic-release 10.7.0; gh-action-pypi-publish 1.14.2; cibuildwheel 4.3.1.
6	
7	## 1. cargo-dist (`dist`)
8	
9	- Phases are CI jobs: plan -> build-local-artifacts (matrix) -> build-global-artifacts -> host -> publish jobs (npm, homebrew, custom) -> announce [D3, D4].
10	- plan emits `dist-manifest.json` ("enumerates the files that builds are expected to produce"; saved, shared between steps and shipped in the release) [D4]. The manifest records the announcement tag, the apps ("releases") and the artifacts [D5]. It has no content hashes of its own that I could confirm. Checksums are sibling `.sha256` files per archive plus a unified `sha256.sum` (since 0.24.0) [D6].
11	- Artifacts move between jobs via `actions/upload-artifact` (`artifacts-build-local-*`, `artifacts-build-global`) and `download-artifact` with `pattern: artifacts-*`. The host job downloads everything and runs `dist host --steps=upload --steps=release` [D3].
12	- Shared effects: "1 Git Tag = 1 dist Announcement = 1 Github Release" [D1]. A human pushes the tag first, and each tag triggers an independent run. The release is one `gh release create <tag> ... artifacts/*` call, commented in source as "upload artifacts transactionally" [D7]. By default it runs in the host job, before the publishers. The docs warn that moving it to announce "is likely to introduce undesirable publishing race conditions", with about 30 seconds in which npm/homebrew installers point at URLs that do not exist yet [D8].
13	- Announce gating: `announce` needs all publish jobs and has `if: always() && needs.host.result == 'success' && (publish-npm.result == 'skipped' || == 'success') ...`. A comment says "use always() && ... to allow us to wait for all publish jobs while still allowing individual publish jobs to skip themselves" [D3]. The `host` job only runs if plan, local and global builds all succeeded or were skipped [D3].
14	- Already-published detection: none found. `publish-npm` loops `npm publish --access public ./npm/$pkg` over the plan with no existence check [D9]. Re-run behavior is unconfirmed: I found no doc on it and no matching issues. Inference: recovery is GitHub's "re-run failed jobs", and a re-run of a half-done npm loop fails on the first package that already exists.
15	- The CI doc says announce creates the final non-draft release [D4], but code and config doc say the default creates it at host [D7, D8].
16	
17	## 2. GoReleaser (and Pro split/merge)
18	
19	- Split/merge is Pro: `goreleaser release --split` builds per GOOS (or target) into `dist/$GOOS`. `goreleaser continue --merge` then "merge[s] previous contexts and artifacts lists", checksums all artifacts, signs, runs "all the publishers" and announcers, and "will not build anything again" [G1]. `publish --merge` and `announce --merge` run separately [G1]. The merge-time checksum covers what the merge job holds. Nothing documented seals the split outputs against what was built (unconfirmed; Pro code is closed).
20	- Publishers run in one fixed ordered list: blob, upload, artifactory, docker, ... then `release.Pipe{}` ("one of the last steps"), then brew/nix/winget/etc. ("brew et al use the release URL, so, they should be last") [G2]. The first failure returns immediately unless the publisher implements `ContinueOnError` and not `--fail-fast`, in which case errors are memoized [G2]. Publishing is skippable via `skips.Publish` [G2]. The docs page on custom publishers says nothing about failure handling [G3].
21	- Release object: "all GitHub releases start as drafts while artifacts are uploaded" [G4]. `CreateRelease` always creates a draft, and `PublishRelease` undrafts only after all uploads succeed [G5]. It first does `findRelease` by tag (or by name among drafts when `use_existing_draft`) and updates in place, else creates [G5]. `replace_existing_draft` deletes same-name drafts first [G4].
22	- Existing asset: an upload that gets 422 fails as unrecoverable unless `replace_existing_artifacts: true`. Then it lists the release's assets, deletes the same-named one and re-uploads, with no hash comparison [G4, G5]. An immutable release fails fast ("already exists and is immutable, it cannot be updated") [G5]. A preflight step checks token and immutability before the build, with `fail_on_error` optional [G2, G4]. `keep_existing_drafts` does not exist in current docs or code (a code search found nothing), so the brief's name is probably `replace_existing_draft`.
23	- The tag is assumed to exist or to be created by the release. `skip_upload` plus an unpushed local tag is documented as a way to "delay the creation of the tag in the remote" [G4].
24	
25	## 3a. release-please
26	
27	- Documented as having no database: "operates without a database of information and so it relies on GitHub as the source of its information" [R1]. State lives in PR labels (`autorelease: pending` -> `tagged`), the manifest file and releases/tags [R1].
28	- Flow: merge release PR -> `createReleases()` creates the GitHub release, which creates the tag at the merge SHA, then relabels the PR as tagged. "release-please is not responsible for publishing your package" [R1]. A duplicate tag is a `DuplicateReleaseError` that is warned about and relabeled [R2].
29	- Known failure: publish steps are gated on `release_created`, which is only true in the run that created the release. After a failed publish, a re-run sees the release, outputs `release_created: false` and skips everything. A user report shows exactly this ("re-running the failed job returned release-please=success with all five publish jobs skipped") [R4]. The action README's only publish pattern is `if: steps.release.outputs.release_created` [R3]. The workaround proposals are `workflow_dispatch` with a tag input, or publish-before-tag. Those come from third-party issues surfaced by search; I did not read all of them (unconfirmed as a general statement).
30	
31	## 3b. Changesets (v3)
32	
33	- `changeset publish` asks the registry per package ("checking if the version ... is published on npm, and if it's not, run npm publish") [C1]. In code, `getUnpublishedPackages` calls `publishTool.info` and includes a package only if `!publishedVersions.includes(localVersion)` [C2].
34	- v3 adds a pack-then-publish flow: `changeset publish-plan --output plan.json`, `changeset pack --out-dir`, `changeset publish --from-pack-dir` [C1, C5]. The plan is versioned (`version: 1`) and chunked by dependency order. Each entry is `publish` with `tarball: {path, integrity}` or `tag-only` [C2]. In artifact mode the publish step reads `publish-plan.json` from the pack dir and does not re-query [C3]. The source comment admits the registry is not recorded in the plan, so the flow "relies on matching configuration values between publish-plan and publish invocations" [C2]. The `--output` format is marked experimental [C1].
35	- Publish semantics: `failed:already-published` is skipped, not fatal [C3]. A hard failure breaks out of all remaining chunks [C3]. Tags are created only for packages that succeeded this run, then existing tags are reported as "Skipped tags (already exist)" [C3, C4]. Exit is 1 if any publish failed, but the tags for the successes are still created [C3].
36	- changesets/action: the publish sub-action reads `git-tag` events from the CLI output, pushes tags via the API and optionally creates a GitHub release per tag, each only for tags created in that run [C6]. `create-github-releases` requires `push-git-tags` [C6].
37	- Inference: a crash after an npm publish but before tagging leaves a public package untagged forever. The next run's plan omits already-published packages, and `tag-only` entries are only generated for private packages [C2, C3].
38	
39	## 4a. semantic-release
40	
41	- Core order: `verifyConditions`, `analyzeCommits`, `verifyRelease`, `generateNotes`, `prepare`, then it creates and pushes the tag, then `publish`. The source comment is "Create the tag before calling the publish plugins as some require the tag to exists" [S1]. The docs do not state this ordering (the plugin docs page is silent) [S3].
42	- `@semantic-release/github` publish: with assets it creates a draft, uploads assets with `Promise.all`, then PATCHes `draft: false` ("so that the assets are available when we get a Github release event") [S2]. An unreadable or non-file asset is logged as an error and ignored, so a partial release can still be published [S2]. A failed upload throws and leaves an orphan draft. There is no existing-asset or existing-release handling in this function [S2].
43	- `--dry-run` skips tag creation and prints notes [S1].
44	- Recovery: none in the tool. The tag is pushed and the next run sees no new commits, so it cannot retry. Third-party sources say the fix is to delete the tag manually; I did not read an official page for this (unconfirmed).
45	
46	## 4b. python-semantic-release
47	
48	- `semantic-release publish --tag <t>` is a separate command that only uploads dists matching `dist_glob_patterns` to an existing release for that tag. It exits 1 if the tag is missing locally [P1]. `version` can create the release, and `create_release` posts `draft: false` then uploads assets afterward. A failed asset upload raises `IncompleteReleaseError` after a public release already exists [P2].
49	- `upload_dists` looks up the release by tag and uploads each file. Failures are aggregated into one `AssetUploadError` listing the HTTP status per file [P2]. A pre-existing asset fails, with no skip and no hash check (inference from absence in the code). PyPI upload is not its job: users run twine or the pypi-publish action.
50	
51	## 5. PyPI guide, cibuildwheel, pypi-publish
52	
53	- Guide: "Keep the build job separate from the publishing jobs. Building distributions in a publishing job is unsupported; publishing jobs should only download the already-built artifacts and upload them." Publishing happens only for a tagged commit [Y1].
54	- cibuildwheel: `build_wheels` matrix plus `build_sdist` upload artifacts named `cibw-*`. Then `upload_pypi: needs: [build_wheels, build_sdist]` downloads `pattern: cibw-*` with `merge-multiple` into `dist/`, and `gh-action-pypi-publish` uploads once with `id-token: write` and an `environment` [Y2, Y3]. Their examples trigger on `release: published`, meaning the GitHub release exists before PyPI. This is the opposite of Callisto's order [Y2, Y3].
55	- pypi-publish README: separate build jobs from publish so you can "(1) test exactly the same artifacts that are about to be uploaded to PyPI, (2) prevent parallel unsynchronized jobs from publishing only part of the dists ... and (3) make an atomic upload" [Y4]. Attestations (PEP 740) are on by default via trusted publishing [Y4, Y5]. `skip-existing` is off by default, with the advice "try to avoid enabling this ... having the former fail loudly on duplicates" [Y4].
56	- `skip-existing` is name-based: twine's `skip_upload` inspects the failed response's status, reason and text for "already exists". It does not compare hashes [Y6].
57	- PyPI never allows reuse. Its three error reasons include "A file with the exact same content exists" and it "does not allow for a filename to be reused, even once a project has been deleted and recreated" [Y7].
58	
59	## (a) Patterns worth copying for Callisto's three questions
60	
61	1. Sealed manifest vs build in publish job. Seal it.
62	   - PyPI's own guide calls building in the publish job "unsupported" [Y1]. Changesets v3 already ships the closest precedent: a versioned plan file holding `{path, integrity}` per tarball, consumed by `publish --from-pack-dir` [C2, C3].
63	   - Go one step further than anyone: the publish job recomputes sha256 of every downloaded file against the manifest, and refuses extra or missing files. cargo-dist has no hash in its plan, and GoReleaser re-checksums at merge, so neither binds publish to build [D6, G1].
64	   - Make the expected set come from the plan, not a glob. Ignored unreadable assets [S2] and a glob that finds fewer wheels than the matrix built both give a short release.
65	2. Rerun with remote files that already exist. Decide by comparing digests, not names.
66	   - Same name and same sha256: done, skip. Same name and different sha256: hard error. PyPI makes this unfixable by re-upload [Y7]. For a draft GitHub release, replace-after-compare is defensible, since GoReleaser's `replace_existing_artifacts` replaces blindly after a 422 [G5].
67	   - `skip-existing` and similar flags treat "exists" as "correct", which is wrong when a rebuild is not byte-identical [Y6]. Unconfirmed: that PyPI's JSON or simple API exposes per-file sha256 for the compare. I know it from general knowledge, not from the pages I fetched.
68	3. Shared effects once per package (tag, release).
69	   - One owner, one tag, one draft release, keyed by tag: GoReleaser's find-by-tag-then-update-else-create over a draft that is only undrafted after uploads is the right shape [G5]. cargo-dist's "1 Tag = 1 Announcement = 1 Release" is the same idea [D1].
70	   - Order: all registries, then tag, then draft release, then assets, then undraft. cargo-dist's `announce` needs-clause (wait for all publishers, treat skipped as ok) is the fan-in to copy [D3]. GoReleaser orders the publishers with the release near the end, because package managers reference the release URL [G2].
71	   - Gate every step on observed state, never on "this run created it". Observed state is the release-please failure mode [R4].
72	   - Immutable releases: check up front (GoReleaser preflight, "already exists and is immutable") [G5, G4]. This is another reason the draft-first order matters.
73	   - Changesets models "tag only" as a plan entry kind in dependency chunks. Callisto can model tag/release/undraft as plan nodes the same way [C2].
74	
75	## (b) Mistakes and limitations to avoid
76	
77	- Tag or release before publish (release-please, semantic-release, PSR, cibuildwheel's `release: published` trigger): a failed publish strands a tag that blocks the retry [R4, S1, P2, Y2].
78	- Success signal that exists for one run only (`release_created`) [R4].
79	- Fire-and-forget upload loops with no existing check (cargo-dist npm loop) [D9].
80	- Silent partial: ignoring unreadable assets [S2], `Promise.all` uploads that leave an orphan draft [S2], and non-draft release then upload (PSR, `IncompleteReleaseError` after publication) [P2].
81	- First failure aborts the remaining publishers (GoReleaser, Changesets) with no "which of the remaining are still unpublished" report [G2, C3]. Callisto's re-derive-and-observe handles this on the next run, but it should still report remaining work on failure.
82	- Blind replace of remote assets [G5], and name-only `skip-existing` [Y6].
83	- Registry not recorded in the plan, so correctness depends on matching config between plan and publish [C2]. Put registry URL, name and version in each sealed op.
84	- GitHub release going public before publishers, creating a window where installers 404 [D8].
85	
86	## (c) Where observe-the-remote, no-journal recovery is stronger or weaker
87	
88	| Tool | Callisto stronger | Callisto weaker |
89	| --- | --- | --- |
90	| cargo-dist | Publish ops are idempotent and re-derived. The announce gate cannot be satisfied by a skipped-but-failed op. | cargo-dist leans on GitHub job-level re-run state and a human-pushed tag as its record. Callisto must re-observe everything. |
91	| GoReleaser | Compares digests instead of blind replace. Treats a failed publisher as "resume", not "abort and delete". | GoReleaser's draft release is itself durable state that survives a crash. Callisto's draft must be found by tag and may have partial assets, so asset listing has to be trusted. |
92	| release-please | Not coupled to "created in this run". Its labels and tags are a journal, and the journal is the failure. | release-please's PR labels give provenance ("this release came from that PR"). A bare registry observation cannot say who published a version. |
93	| Changesets | Covers the publish-then-crash-before-tag window (inference: Changesets can miss it for public packages [C2, C3]). | Changesets is the same shape (observe registry) and ships a sealed plan with `integrity`. Callisto matches it only if its manifest verifies hashes. |
94	| semantic-release / PSR | Can retry at all. | Their tag is the one-bit journal. |
95	| PyPI pattern | Adds the digest compare that `skip-existing` lacks. | PyPI's atomicity story is "one upload job". Callisto's multi-registry DAG has no atomic multi-registry step, so partial states are normal and must be reported. |
96	
97	Weaknesses specific to no-journal recovery:
98	- Observation shows that a version exists, not that this intent put it there. Mitigate with the sealed sha256 compare, and treat a mismatch as a hard stop. Do not "adopt" it.
99	- Observation lags: registry or CDN caches can show a version absent just after publish. A retry then hits "already exists" errors. Treat duplicate-error plus a matching digest as success.
100	- If the committed decision changes between runs (new files in the build), the re-derived plan differs from the first attempt. A sealed manifest tied to the decision's hash fixes this: a changed manifest means a new attempt, not a resume.
101	
102	## Sources
103	
104	- [D1] https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/book/src/reference/concepts.md
105	- [D3] https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/cargo-dist/templates/ci/github/release.yml.j2
106	- [D4] https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/book/src/ci/index.md
107	- [D5] https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/book/src/reference/schema.md
108	- [D6] https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/book/src/artifacts/checksums.md
109	- [D7] https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/cargo-dist/src/backend/ci/github.rs and .../templates/ci/github/partials/publish_github.yml.j2
110	- [D8] https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/book/src/reference/config.md (github-release)
111	- [D9] https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/blob/main/cargo-dist/templates/ci/github/partials/publish_npm.yml.j2
112	- [G1] https://github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/blob/main/www/content/customization/general/partial.md
113	- [G2] https://github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/blob/main/internal/pipe/publish/publish.go and .../internal/pipeline/pipeline.go
114	- [G3] https://goreleaser.com/customization/publishers/
